catalog_quote: Three degrees of stress (primary, secondary, and 'zero') are found in surface forms.[3] Pitch is not contrastive within lexical items: the syntactical function of pitch is badly understood as yet. [fn. 3] Although, for dictionary items, only primary stress (and its position) need be indicated. [p. 127] First, it is noted that many disyllabic stems, in citation as well as in the texts, have freely alternating stress.[1] Such are xʷesqam 'few'; ɬokʷaɬ 'moon, sun; s-ʔobat 'name'; sedaq 'fly'; p̓estab 'all, everything.' ... The expression 'allomorphy of stress' implies that we assign the alternation to the dictionary entry itself. But this is by no means an inevitable choice. [fn. 1] But compare ʔélal 'sing'; ʔelál 'weep'; bə́təb 'murdered'; bətə́b 'warm'; [p. 53, Rule Summary 1] 2. In the environment of the augment, stress retracts to the stem-initial syllable. Stress on an originally-stressed non-initial syllable in the stem falls to secondary stress. [p. 72] For di-syllabic stems with primary stress on the first syllable (type š-čótax̣; š-čt-čótax̣ 'halibut'), the stress-retraction rule operates vacuously on the augmented form ... For di-syllabic stems with primary stress on the second syllable (type təbéxʷ; təb-tábaxʷ 'land'), the stress is retracted in the augment [pp. 275-276] Fig. 78.--Roots CV́CVC ... Fig. 79.--Roots CVCV́C

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress is a lexical property of each dictionary item: disyllabic and CVCVC roots are listed as either initial-stressed (sídakʷ 'sea', túkʷad 'moon', čúcid 'mouth') or final-stressed (ʔabít 'stand', ʔupát 'eat', tebíxʷ 'land'), with minimal pairs (ʔélal 'sing' vs ʔelál 'weep'; bátab 'murdered' vs batáb 'warm'). Morphology then moves it: in the Augment (plural) reduplication stress retracts to the stem-initial syllable and the original stressed vowel keeps secondary stress and ablauts to a; in the Attenuative (diminutive) stress goes to the prefix (or to the stem's first vowel in laryngeal-final stems); in ʔ/h-final stems stress may optionally shift to the suffix -as 'possessive' / -ab 'verbalizer'. Many disyllabic stems show free stress alternation. Pitch is not contrastive.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Explicitly recognized: three degrees (primary, secondary, zero); secondary stress is what an originally stressed non-initial stem syllable keeps after augment stress-retraction, and it conditions the vowel-ablaut to a (pp. 49-50, 53).
new_statements.exceptions: Free stress alternation in many disyllabic stems ('stress allomorphy', p.127: x̌ʷesqam 'few', tokʷad 'moon, sun', s-ʔobat 'name'); augmented forms where retraction fails ('Not Retraction Rule', p.128); 'secondary shift' back to the unaugmented stem stress (p.129); stressed reduplication in 'canes', 'babies' (p.130); optional stress shift to suffix in laryngeal-final stems (p.96); analogical stress-shift in the Attenuative (p.158).
new_statements.domain_note: Word/stem level, from elicited single words and citation forms (word lists) plus texts; the author notes that text intonation and overlength vowels are 'often completely at odds with the conception of stress and stress-alternation gained in the eliciting of single words' (p. 20). Language is dormant (spoken 'until the early years of the present century', p.1); data from one main speaker, Louise Pulsifer, field-work 1960s.
new_statements.identity_note: Drachman 1969 describes Twana as spoken by the Skokomish (his main consultant Louise Pulsifer, 'oldest living member of the Skokomish tribe'); Twana = Skokomish, twan1247, no separate dialect issue. The earlier scan's 'the named source could not be reached' classification is overturned: the OSU Linguistics department serves the full WPL 5 scan openly (kb.osu.edu itself could not be reached by automated download).
